utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic and Vladimir Santic, also known as "Vlado."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. Mr. Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The Prosecutor wants to call three witnesses this morning, Mr. Lee Whitworth, Dr. Van der Peijl, and then Witness 8. I ask that Mr. Whitworth be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Krajina? It's not our fault. All the accused should be here on time. If they are not on time, we will start, as long as some of them are here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are all the accused here, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I call Mr. Lee Whitworth. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Will you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Mr. Smith?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Smith:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Whitworth. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are currently a school teacher in England; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to that, you used to be in the British army?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You served in Bosnia in 1993?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I did, indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which regiment did you serve with?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I served with the 1st Battalion, the Prince of Wales' Own Regiment of Yorkshire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long had you been in the British army prior to that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Approximately three years, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you on any other operational tours in that time?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Prior to deploying to Bosnia, I worked in Belfast for approximately seven months and was involved in the OP Granby building and training phases as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain what that is, please?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That is the training and deployment for the Gulf, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What period were you in Bosnia in 1993?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: From approximately the middle of May until, I think it was, the beginning of November, middle of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your rank?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I was a captain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you been to officer training school in Sandhurst, in England, when you first joined the British army?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court your main job when you were in Bosnia and where you were based?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Initially, I was deployed as the regimental signals officer which was responsible for setting up and running the headquarters element. Very quickly after our arrival, Colonel Alastair started to understand the need for good liaison on the ground, and so he tested myself and a few of the other officers as liaison officers in order to build a rapport with the locals in the Lasva Valley area. I was retasked from regimental signals officer as a liaison officer in the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You commenced your tour in May, and you took over from the Cheshire Regiment that had just completed theirs?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the specific nature of your job in relation of liaison? What types of people were you aiming at liaising with and the purpose for that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: We were really there to facilitate the UNHCR, the UN Mission in the Lasva Valley, and we really perceived that as taking form of establishing a rapport and relationship with all senior people on the ground in the Lasva Valley area; political, military, civilian leaders. Establishing a rapport and relationship with them would then allow us to support and facilitate the movement of UNHCR vehicles in and out of the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the area that you covered, what municipalities?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: There were four liaison officers. My area of responsibility was from Travnik through the Vitez Lasva Valley as far as the Busovaca area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You met and liaised with military leaders from the Bosnian army and the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, sir, civilian, political, and military leaders on both sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst you were doing this during this time, did you come to meet and know Vladimir Santic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes. I think I met him on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the first date that you met Vladimir Santic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was quite early on in my tour, around the end of May, beginning of June, and I was trying to establish key personalities in the Lasva Valley area. On this particular occasion, I had gone looking for senior Military Police representatives in the Vitez area. I first met Mr. Santic under the guise of being a senior military policeman in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of which military group?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He was lodged at 4th Battalion Military Police headquarters in the Hotel Vitez when I met him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's the HVO, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What gave you reason to go and meet him? What happened earlier that day that led you to go to the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: As I said, I think earlier, during the beginning of my tour, I was spending a lot of time driving around the area, introducing myself to people, just trying to become familiar with the circumstances and the situation that people were in and trying to identify who the key personalities were in the area. I'd happened along the road heading towards Zenica, and I came across a building that we came to know as the Swiss Cottage or the Bungalow. On the front porch of that building, there was a group of about eight to ten soldiers, quite distinctly dressed. So I took the opportunity to pull up and try to engage them in conversation. They were not very welcoming at first. They obviously weren't interested in speaking to me at the time. After about a 20-minute, 30-minute conversation, I said to them that it would be useful for me in my role as a liaison officer, in order to help the humanitarian mission, if I was to introduce myself to their commander. There was a gentleman who kept coming out the back of the Bungalow who was obviously more senior than the young gentlemen I was talking to in the front, and he was not very pleased about the fact that they were having a general conversation with me. Nevertheless, they said, "You need to speak to our boss. He's a chap called Pasko. You'll find him down in Vitez." It was with that that I set off to Vitez looking for the leader of these group of gentlemen who had described themselves as an elite Military Police unit that had been active and involved in all the military successes in the Lasva Valley area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe, more specifically, any type of weaponry that was at the Bungalow and the types of uniforms they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes. They were very distinctly dressed. They were all dressed in black. They were young, between the age, I would say, of 25, 26, fit, athletic-looking chaps, predominantly dressed in black, as opposed to the normals of Croatian-type, U.S. uniforms that were common. They were all wearing small arms, usually one or two large knives. There were plenty of weapons propped up in the doorway and on the inside of the building, wearing bandannas. They were proud of this elite Military Police status that they had. They were all very confidant at the time. They were proud of the fact that they had been involved in the military successes that they reiterated to me at the time that had taken place in the Lasva Valley area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once that was explained to you, that they were proud of the fact that they were involved in the military successes in the Lasva Valley area, did you follow up on that comment?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I attempted to do so, yes. It's obviously a difficult situation. It was quite clear to me that one of the gentleman there, who was obviously the senior rank present, wasn't happy about them disclosing any information to me. It was something that I approached very delicately, and I said to them, "You mean like operations like Ahmici?" They didn't deny or acknowledge that, but they said -- the phrase that they used was, "We said all the military successes." That intimated to me that that was an indirect acknowledgement of the fact that they had been involved in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you mention Ahmici? What was your knowledge, just briefly, of what had occurred there?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was, I think, six weeks prior to that particular incident. It was an event that had, obviously, stuck in everybody's minds of the Cheshires and the Prince of Wales' Own. It was something we were all aware of in the background; that really was quite a key operation in the Lasva Valley. It was the most obvious one, the most striking one, to ask them about at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how far was this Bungalow from Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Approximately 500, 600 metres. There's a wood that separates the area of Ahmici from the Bungalow area, so it was quite close.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Towards Vitez or away from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was away from Vitez, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that these young men were wearing black uniforms. Did you notice whether they had any patches on?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I didn't notice any insignia -- oh, I did, actually, report that some of them had what looked like basic insignia on their arms, and they referred to themselves as the Jokers. "The Jokeri" was the name that they gave to me at the time. Whilst I was there, I had a Muslim interpreter, and she was very fearful. She said, "These gentlemen were very dangerous." I think I mentioned earlier that when I initially tried to make conversation with them, they were quite aggressive and focused in on my Muslim interpreter at the time. It was only after I had gone to considerable lengths to put them at ease that they actually managed to converse with me. But she impressed upon me that she was fearful of them and that she'd heard of this name before and that they were involved in several military operations in the Lasva Valley area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that Exhibit 119 be produced to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court whether you can identify that building in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I can, indeed, yes, and the gentlemen out front. That was the building we referred to as the Swiss Cottage or the Swiss Bungalow. The balcony on the front there is where I had the conversation with the chaps. There's a large square door there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see inside the square door when you had the conversation with these men?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was dark inside, but it just had wooden furniture and benches lining the sides and weapons propped up. It was quite a spacious building. I don't think there was anything else on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This conversation went for about 20 minutes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice whether there was any damage to the building when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No. That didn't appear to be the case. I saw no signs of small arms or any other damage there on the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you left this group and went to Hotel Vitez, what was your impression of the group? What type of group, in military terms, would you classify them as?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They seemed very well-motivated. They were very well-equipped. They were very confidant in the fact that -- they were very confidant in their own ability. I'd come away with an impression that this was a group of chaps who were, actually, involved in offensive action in the Lasva Valley area, that they were directly responsible, or I was assuming they were directly responsible for the offensive action in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were told that their commander was Pasko, and you went to Vitez. What was your aim at that stage?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Simply to introduce myself to their commander. They had told me they were an elite Military Police unit, and I'd said to them that it would be useful, therefore, if I was to introduce myself to their commander. They had reluctantly given me this name, and I set off into the Vitez area looking for a senior military policeman, this chap called Pasko. I went to the Hotel Vitez, and I spoke to a couple of members of the HVO there. I told them I had this conversation with the Jokeri. It was still during the early days of my role as a liaison officer, so I sort of talked them around to the idea that it was in the interests of everybody in the Lasva Valley area that I meet all the key personnel. I said, "Could I speak to the senior Military Police commander?" I sat down. After awhile, a gentleman came out who introduced himself to me as Vlado. He was introduced to me as the senior Military Police commander in the area, but no specific title was given to me at that time. He just came out in response to my request for a senior military policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stopping there. Why did you go to Hotel Vitez? What did you believe Hotel Vitez to be?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Well, I had already been introduced to one or two characters in the Hotel Vitez. I was aware that that's where the HVO military command was situated, and I was looking for a Military Police commander. It seemed common sense to go to the hotel. There is, actually, a big sign above the door that says "4th Battalion Military Police Headquarters," so it was just common sense, really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the first person who you first asked at Hotel Vitez in relation to your request to see the commander of the Jokers?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think it was a chap called Darko Gelic, who was later tasked as Colonel Blaskic's personal liaison officer. I got to know Darko throughout the following months quite well, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you met this man that came out in response to your request, can you give a description of him?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes. Stockily built, going very thin on the top, white-greyish hair, about 5'10".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, he was wearing a Military Police -- he had combat trousers, a green shirt on. My memory is a little bit hazy of such details. I have no reason to think that he wasn't the military policeman that I'd asked for at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he introduce himself?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: In a very cursory manner. He was very disinterested in me. I did try and win him over. I sort of chatted to him. I did most of the talking. He was very incommunicative, didn't really see me as anybody of any importance and didn't really see the need for him to establish a rapport with me. For the 10 minutes, 15 minutes that I was talking to him, I did most of the talking and I was trying to explain the situation and the merits of the UN and my role in that and how I might be able to assist him, as a policeman, in observing and facilitating the UN mission in the area. He sat and listened, was pretty unforthcoming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you mention to him why you were there, the fact that you had been to the Bungalow earlier?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I did, indeed. I said that I'd spoke to a Military Police group. That was always a way of brokering a conversation with people, in that people were always very distrustful of why you wanted to know. So it was always useful to have a name to be able to say, "I have already spoken to so and so." Yes, I did mention that at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you mention the name "The Jokers" at the time?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, I did so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he say in response to that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I don't remember him saying anything, if I was to be honest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was fairly reluctant to speak to you for that ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, he was. I would say he was very unforthcoming, didn't really want to make conversation with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you left that meeting, were you subsequently introduced to a person called Pasko?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was a month, two months later, I was formally introduced to a man called Pasko Ljubicic by Darko Gelic, the liaison officer, who introduced him as head of the 4th Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your experience and observations in the Lasva Valley over that six months, where did Santic sit in comparison to Pasko Ljubicic? Where did Vladimir Santic sit?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: At the time when I initially met Mr. Santic, it seemed obvious to me that he was subordinate to Pasko, this chief of the Military Police Battalion. We weren't exactly sure in what role he was subordinate, whether he was within the 4th Military Battalion or maybe commanding one of the sub-units within the 4th Military Battalion. I was aware, speaking to people at the time, that Mr. Santic was a local man, local to Vitez, but at that particular time, we didn't really know where he was, other than being, say, somewhere underneath the command structure -- within the command structure of Pasko Ljubicic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain the structure of the Military Police Battalion, the units that it was divided up into, and the general area that you believed it to cover, the 4th Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: This is information that became apparent to us throughout the tour. It wasn't initially apparent on my first meeting with Mr. Santic, but it became obvious that the Military Police sub-units, as we referred to them, were based on municipalities, and that the 4th Military Police battalion actually covered a large area. The area it covered, I think, corresponded with the op zone, the HVO Operational Zone, included places like Vares, Zepce, Busovaca, Travnik, Novi Travnik, Vitez. The information and conversations that I had throughout suggested that the 4th Military Battalion was also spread out over a similar area. In each of those municipalities, there would be a sub-unit, a company group, we would call them, in each of those. So there would be a company group within Vitez, a company group of the 4th Battalion within Vares, within Zepce, within Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pasko Ljubicic was introduced to you as the commander of that whole area?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He was, indeed, sir, yes. At the time when I met the Jokeri, he was just introduced to me by the Jokeri as their commander. That was all they said. Of course, that's an assumption that the Pasko that they were referring to, because they didn't give me a second name, was the Pasko Ljubicic who was commander of the 4th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Military Police company that was located in the Vitez municipality, from your observations and your dealings with the HVO in '92, '93, where would you put Vladimir Santic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Well, it's commonplace for a headquarters unit, for a battalion headquarters, to be co-located with one of the company groups for its own protection and the facilities that are, therefore, provided. I was aware that Mr. Santic was within the HVO structure in the hotel. At the time when I actually met him, it wasn't clear whether he was a company commander of the local Vitez Military Police situated in the hotel or whether he was actually part of Pasko Ljubicic's battalion headquarters staff and subordinate to him in that way, located in the Hotel Vitez. But knowing that he was a local Vitez man, I wouldn't like to say, really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned each municipality had a company-sized unit of the Military Police based there. About what size would that be in relation to the Vitez Military Police?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: A company group normally would be, approximately, 120, 140 soldiers in a conventional army grouping, but, obviously, circumstances are very different. From what I saw, driving up and down 12, 14 hours a day in the Lasva Valley, I would say the numbers of a Military Police company compared favourably with that. So you were looking at 100-plus troops within a Military Police company. There were similar sized groups within each area; Busovaca, Travnik, Novi Travnik. It also appeared, but it's difficult to put an exact figure on it because, of course, all the troops are on duty, and very rarely would you see groups of more than two or three together at a time, but, obviously, driving up and down the valley every day, you're sampling or you're seeing small groups here and there, and they are, obviously, representative of those who are on duty for that particular time of day. There were instances when I saw 30-plus together when senior dignitaries were visiting, like Cedric Thornbird, at the Nova Bila Hospital. It was obvious that they were a quite sizeable number, and it was reasonably comparable to that 100-plus that you would see in a normal company group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What size was the Jokers, the special elite Military Police unit that you were told about?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: From the initial conversation I'd had with them, they said they were of a number of approximately 30-plus, that there were quite a number of them. That would be a platoon, small sub-unit size, a sub-unit of a company. In a company group, you would find four of those grouped under a company commander. They were, obviously, a small unit within the Military Police structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke to the group of men that claimed that they were the Jokers, they boasted about the fact that they were involved in all the successful military operations in the Lasva Valley. Can you tell the Court, based on your observations in Bosnia for that six months, whether or not a person in Pasko Ljubicic's position, and also Vladimir Santic's position, would have necessarily needed to be involved in the planning and organising of those operations?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Can you make specific reference to -- could you ask the question again, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the Jokers were an active military unit, you thought, and they claimed that they -- in fact, they were involved in all the successful military operations in the Lasva Valley. Can you tell the Court, based on your opinion down there, whether or not it would be necessary for a person at the level of Vladimir Santic or Pasko Ljubicic to be involved in the planning and organising of any of the significant military operations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Mr. President, I have an objection to make with regard to this examination. From the direct answer given by this witness, he did not differentiate between the relationship of Vlado Santic and Pasko Ljubicic. He did not bring Vlado Santic into any relationship with the latter, and he said that he belonged to the local structures within the HVO, the command of which was located at the Hotel Vitez. Therefore, a question of this nature suggests that between these two individuals there was a necessary link which, in that case, makes up a chain. I think that by saying so, the witness is being suggested something which he did not previously state when speaking about the relationship between the two individuals mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I wonder whether, Mr. Smith, you could rephrase your question. I see a lot of merit in the objection of Counsel Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps if I can try and ask the witness if he could establish that relation between Pasko Ljubicic and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Try it and refrain from asking hypothetical questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Darko Gelic was the liaison officer for Mr. Blaskic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Blaskic was the commander of the third operative zone of the HVO in Central Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you dealt with Darko Gelic on a fairly frequent basis as a liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Three, four times a day on most days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he inform you of the relationship between Pasko Ljubicic and Vladimir Santic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: His words were, that it was from him that he said that Mr. Santic was the senior Military Police commander in the Vitez area, and no specifics were given other than Pasko Ljubicic was his commander as in terms of the battalion commander. So I think, as I said earlier, its's very difficult to push for specifics, but in any normal change of command in the military, there will be direct communication. I think to answer the question you said earlier about Jokeri involvement and any connection between the two, it would be very difficult not to see a connection in terms of any military operations that took place in the Lasva Valley, would have been strategically directed and would have had to have local command involved in their occurrence in the Lasva Valley area. So I think -- I'm going around a long way of saying I saw no direct, specific connection between the two, other than to say that it was -- I was told at the time that one was subordinate to the other, but how -- the specifics of that subordination was not made clear to me at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I would like a video to be played, Prosecution Exhibit 253. On this video, can you tell the Court whether you can recognise the location and any figures that appear within it?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Would you like me to ask for video to be stopped?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you recognise anything in the video, the location or the personalities within it, if you could ask for the video to be stopped. I'll just ask that the usher could organise that the video appears on the witness's screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps my intervention has come too early, but would it be a good idea for the Prosecutor to tell us where the tape is from and how he came by it before we see the actual tape?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, this was already explained by the Prosecutor on a previous occasion. This is already an exhibit, a Prosecution Exhibit. Do you remember? You will see. If you wait a few seconds, you will see.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I apologise then. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stop it there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is that person in the frame?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That was a man who was formally introduced to me by Darko Gelic as Pasko Ljubicic, commander of the 4th Battalion Military Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Could we continue with the tape, please? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you stop it there, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise anyone in that frame?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the quality of the picture, that -- I'm not as sure as I can be. That would be Vladimir Santic, with his hand on his head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was the person who was introduced to you at the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He was indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If you could continue the tape, please, and I'll ask you a few questions after that. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If you can stop the tape now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you recognise the location of where that footage was taken?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Very difficult. It could possibly have been in the cottage by the nature of the vertical slat walls, but the quality is obviously very poor. I wouldn't swear on oath to that at all, but it could possibly have been inside the cottage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that because of the nature of the frame within the video clip?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yeah. It was almost vertically sided. There were benches pushed up against the side. Large chunky wooden furniture inside, that type of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could take a look around the courtroom and tell the Court whether or not you could recognise Vladimir Santic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I can indeed, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you point him out to the Court?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He's sat over there smiling at me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I ask the Court to accept that --

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He's wearing a subtle lilac shirt with a striped tie and a dark blue blazer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: For the record, I ask the Court that the witness had identified the accused Vladimir Santic. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. Mr. Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. No questions from any legal Defence counsel? All right. So there will be no re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. So I think there's no objection to the witness being released. Thank you so much for coming here to give evidence in court. You may now be released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I assume we are now moving on to the Dutch -- it will be even shorter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Exactly, Mr. President. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. I would like to ask you to read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Terrier:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, witness. Could you tell the court what your name is and what your occupation is?

utterances.speaker: GERHARD VAN DER PEIJL
utterances.text: My name is Gerhard van der Piejl. I'm a forensic scientist at the forensic science laboratory of the Ministry of the Netherlands -- Ministry of Justice of the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In June 1998, you carried out a number of tests on items and samples that had been collected in a Bosnian village, and they had been transmitted to you by Mr. Prudon; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GERHARD VAN DER PEIJL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You signed an analysis report dated 29th of July, 1998. This report has been tendered as Exhibit 169, and I shall ask the witness that the Dutch version and its translation in English be submitted to the court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit 278, 278A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Van der Peijl, while I'm showing this to you, I would like to ask you whether the English translation of your conclusions, to be more specific, seems to be an accurate one?

utterances.speaker: GERHARD VAN DER PEIJL
utterances.text: In the conclusion it says, in the English version, that there were no combustion enhancing substances in fire samples et cetera. Actually, in the Dutch version it says no accelerants were detected in the samples, et cetera. That's in the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you concluded that you did not find any accelerants in the test?

utterances.speaker: GERHARD VAN DER PEIJL
utterances.text: That's the main difference. There are some other smaller ones, but I don't think they are relevant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we won't go into them then. I have only one question, but it is a major one for you. It is as follows: The fact that you did not detect any inflammable substance during the test, does that mean that no inflammable substance had been used in order to fire, or to burn the place where the samples were found, were collected? You may not know this, and there was no reason for telling you that then, but the fire took place on the 16th of April, 1993. The samples were collected in July, 1998. The site on which the samples were collected was open -- was an open space and was weather-beaten all these years.

utterances.speaker: GERHARD VAN DER PEIJL
utterances.text: From my -- especially from my own experience but also from literature, I don't know any studies about what will happen to accelerants if they are in open weather places, perhaps in the ground for such a long time. There have been some studies, for example, on microbacterial degradation of gasoline, especially in Australia, and they have demonstrated that in some cases there could be major degradation, but that's only shorter-term studies. So I cannot say what could happen with an accelerant in so long a time. The thing is, though, that although I don't have any studies -- or I should say I don't know, but I think I -- still from my experience and my chemical knowledge, I can make a conclusion. There are three possibilities that I can imagine where we would not find any traces of accelerants today, even though they might have been used five years ago for arson, and that would be for the first reason -- the first reason will be that the samples that have been taken were not actually samples where accelerant has been present at the start. Like the name says, an accelerant is used to accelerate the fire. But when the fire has started, of course it can go burn further on if you have wood and some our combustible material. You may have even charred or burned material where no accelerant is present. So that depends whether people have been able to take the accelerants at the place where the fire really started. The second possibility is that -- that's all assuming an accelerant was used in the first place, of course. The second possibility is that an accelerant has been used which consists of very volatile components. For example, in the Netherlands we would think then about mixture of alcohol. In Dutch we call it bronspiritus. It's very common in the household. You could have a mixture of paint thinner, some paint thinners. They are very volatile. I would not expect, after so long a time, that we would find any trace of them. Normally, even after a shorter time, we find traces of more -- of liquids which have less volatile components in them. For example, for gasoline, over 99 per cent of gasoline would be evaporated after a few days, but 1 per cent remaining may still lead us to conclude that there has been gasoline in the sample. Or with diesel fuel, that's another possibility. So when I was originally asked the question to look for accelerants in these samples, I said already I can only find accelerants if it has been some of this group. That means that if I don't find any accelerants, one of the possibilities, of course, then, that it's from outside of this group. The third possibility, I already touched on it, is there has been such heavy microbacterial degradation over this long period of time, that that is the reason we don't find anything. So to conclude again, there are three main possibilities. One is that the samples were taken not at the place where the accelerant was originally used. The second is that an accelerant has been used which consisted of very volatile components and no less volatile components have remained. The third possibility is that there has been microbacterial deterioration. So in these three cases and perhaps more but -- that's, I think what I want to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't want the interpreter service to be angry at me, but I'm afraid we cannot understand the interpretation. And if possible, we would like another interpreter to replace the present one who is interpreting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: This is the interpretation from English into Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, into Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I hope somebody in the booth can replace the present interpreter. Counsel Radovic, do you want now -- do you want Mr. Terrier to ask again the last question?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: We are investing great efforts to understand and follow what has been said. What we did not understand, we shall clarify later on in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: At any rate, I want to thank the witness for what he has said. I have no further questions for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have one question, and Mr. Ranko Radovic and Ms. Jadranka Slokovic-Glumac have questions. Cross-examined by Mr. Pavkovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I have one question for you and it is the following: In the samples that you were given, and which you, therefore, analysed, did you find the presence of any accelerators of any kind or combustion enhancing substances?

utterances.speaker: GERHARD VAN DER PEIJL
utterances.text: No, I did not find any presence of what we call an accelerant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Pavkovic. Counsel Radovic? Cross-examined by Mr. Radovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I shall continue the topic that my learned colleague Mr. Pavkovic started. The Prosecutor asked you, sir, how is it possible that no combustion enhancing substances were detected? As a forensic scientist, is it usual for you to explain why these substances were not found, or is it the job of a forensic scientist just to determine whether these substances exist or not? What is the basic task of a forensic scientist of your kind?

utterances.speaker: GERHARD VAN DER PEIJL
utterances.text: Okay. The last word in the English translation is "of your kind," and that will give what is my expertise. In the Netherlands we have different expertise for the people who do chemical investigations, that's people like me, and people who do technical investigations and the investigations at the scene of a possible crime. In other countries, this job can be combined in one person, but in the Netherlands we have decided to split it up. Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. In my country, the system is similar. My question was: Is it the basic task of a forensic scientist to determine whether the combustion enhancing substances exist, or accelerants, or whether it is his task to explain why he did not find elements of this kind in the samples received?

utterances.speaker: GERHARD VAN DER PEIJL
utterances.text: Okay. Normally I would just make out report as I have done it over here, and in the Dutch court our Judges, and advocates and Prosecutors, they are aware of what that means, that no -- if no accelerant has been found, it definitely does not mean that no accelerant has been used. In this case, for this International Court, I have been asked by the Prosecutor to come over here and to expand on my report, to clarify that even though we did not find -- we did not detect any accelerant, any trace of accelerant, it definitely does not mean that no accelerant has been used at the fire in the past.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the reasons for which this kind of conclusion is possible, and your finding is possible as it stands, is that the individual taking the samples might not have taken the samples from the right place. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: GERHARD VAN DER PEIJL
utterances.text: That is correct. It could mean, for example, that he could not take the samples from the right place, because if the right place would have been burned out completely, if there would have been a major fire, that also can happen in Dutch, we might not even find anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the individual taking the samples, according to the proceedings so far, is an individual who is the supreme investigator on the part of the Dutch police who went on the spot, and he was informed of the witness testimony when the witness said -- stated the spot where the burning took place. In a situation of this kind, is there very little probability that the sample sent to you for expertise was not taken from the proper place?

utterances.speaker: GERHARD VAN DER PEIJL
utterances.text: This -- this person, this Mr. Prudon, is of a good reputation to me from the past. As far as I know, he has also been certified for the technical police to do these arson investigations, and I would expect that he would be able to get the most out of it. But if no sample is left over from -- from an accelerant because everything has been burned out, then, of course, he could not have taken the sample which contains the accelerant. Another possibility is -- I have not seen photographs of the situation -- I'll wait for a moment. I have not seen photographs of the situation at the point, but I have understood that there has been -- I think you call it a cave-in of the building. There's a lot of rubble. In that situation that may present some problems. Normally what an investigator would look for in the Dutch case where he normally comes in after only a few days, he would look for -- for example, for cardboard, or a desk office or for something else which has not been burnt out completely. If that is in the neighbourhood of the fire, he would look underneath, for example, a table leg or something like that, because there you have the best chance to find any residues of an accelerant because it has been sort of shielded from the heat of the fire. That's what you would do in a normal situation. As far as I understand, but you have here the witness, I think, there was a problem in this situation to do something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other reason that you quoted, which prevented results of your expertise being exact, is that there was a -- that a combination was used of different chemical matter. Did I understand you correctly in saying that?

utterances.speaker: GERHARD VAN DER PEIJL
utterances.text: Okay. There are many possible accelerants. Accelerants, they are fluids which -- they are very easy to make -- how do you call it -- to make into a fire. In the Dutch situation, in cases where we find an accelerant, for example, in about half of the cases, we find something like petrol being used. But in the Netherlands' situation and also abroad, there are many accelerants which can be used, and one of the possibilities I gave to you is a mixture of volatile alcohols. In the Netherlands that's definitely being used. I don't know the market situation in the former Yugoslavia, if it is possible to get something like that. That's one possibility, and I'm quite sure we wouldn't find any traces of that because they would be very volatile, and also, they would be oxidised over the years, so I would not expect to find anything. Another possibility is some paint thinners. They also consist only of very volatile components, and I would not expect to find anything. The ones I would expect -- no, no, I should say differently. The ones which in principle might leave some residue are things like diesel fuel. I would have hoped that even if diesel fuel was used, even after all these years and even though nobody ever did a scientific investigation for an arson case, it might have been possible that we would have found traces of some of the components from this diesel fuel. But there are many other possibilities of accelerants where I would not have expected to find a trace after such a long period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have given us a very good explanation now of the different theoretical possibilities. However, I don't know whether you were doing your expertise, that you were drawing our attention to the fact that an individual claimed to be an eyewitness and said that petrol was used. Now, what is the situation like with petrol?

utterances.speaker: GERHARD VAN DER PEIJL
utterances.text: Sorry, can you say it again? As an eyewitness who says petrol has been used?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that petrol was used. Now, I'm interested in knowing your opinion with regard to traces of petrol, if petrol was what was used as an accelerator at the initial spot for planting the fire?

utterances.speaker: GERHARD VAN DER PEIJL
utterances.text: Yeah. First of all, I definitely wasn't aware that there was a witness saying that petrol had been used. Like I said already, even when petrol would have been used, we would --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Please, one moment. Mr. Terrier wants --

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radovic. I would just like to point out, maybe belatedly, that I don't have the feeling that the witness mentioned by Mr. Radovic had mentioned the chemical composition of the product that was used on his house. I don't think that he had mentioned the use of petrol used for cars, as was pointed out just now by Mr. Radovic, but I don't have anything against the question being asked, because indeed, if the question is asked it is only a hypothetical one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, but it's worth asking the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Quite. It's only a hypothetical question raised by Mr. Radovic then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but the man that I am thinking of, I forget whether he is a witness or not so I'm not going to mention his name, but he did mention petrol. Of course, he did not say whether it was the super type of gasoline or the ordinary type, but he did speak about bottles of petrol, and that is why I'm asking that as a possibility, and I'd like to hear the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: GERHARD VAN DER PEIJL
utterances.text: Okay. So as a possibility, a theoretical possibility, in -- first of all, I should say, as far as I know there are no scientific studies to see what happens after so long a period of time when you leave petrol. I know that for shorter periods of time, of course, in a few days already normally most of the petrol will have been evaporated unless it is shielded well down below in the ground and you have a better position. But normally most of it will have been evaporated and you will end up with, say, roughly one per cent of the original petrol being used is left over. Then what can happen is especially if it is in the ground area, what you can get is that you get microbacterial -- microbacteria from the soils which attack the chemical components. Although in the Netherlands, even though in some of these studies we have looked for it we didn't find so much of it, I know definitely there are several studies of degradation of the materials which are much shorter than the period of five years I have understood in this case. There you see the pattern completely disappears, pattern of components, relative concentrations we would use to identify something as petrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Would the expert witness please repeat the last sentence, because the interpreter said that he did not catch it, so would the gentlemen please repeat his last sentence?

utterances.speaker: GERHARD VAN DER PEIJL
utterances.text: Okay. I don't know if I can do it literally, but the point is I gave three possibilities -- I gave three possibilities for -- we could not find any trace of accelerants now even though an accelerant has been used. For petrol it might be this -- the first case that the samples were taken from the wrong position, or, and I expounded on that the last time, that microbacterial deterioration has, you might say, eaten up the components of petrol which was originally used in this hypothetical, theoretical situation. I have some scientific literature to support it, that that could have happened, even on a much shorter time scale than five years' time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us conclude our examination now. Do you agree, then, that the results of your analysis would be the following: By a scientific method, it has not been proved that on the spot traces were found of substances which would be used as accelerants or combustion-enhancing substances which would lead to a fire?

utterances.speaker: GERHARD VAN DER PEIJL
utterances.text: Yes. By scientific methods, no traces were detected of substances which could be used as, what I see over here, combustion-enhancing substances.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Radovic. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I have no questions either. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much for coming to give evidence. You may now be released. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The next witness will be Witness 8; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Exactly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes. We do ask for protective measures, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It was not specified on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: It is not specified on the list, Your Honour, but the witness asks for protection of her name and of her face.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Then it will be Witness FF, double "F"?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. It will be Witness FF.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, we would like to take a pause in about 30-minutes' time. I think that maybe you will be able to complete your direct examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Maybe, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Okay, maybe. Then maybe in 30 minutes, we'll take a break, and maybe afterwards we'll go on to cross-examination. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam. Could you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Terrier:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam. I'm going to give to the usher a piece of paper on which your name appears. Please tell us if this is your name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 279.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, the Judges have granted you a number of protective measures, measures which you have asked for. Your face and your name will be protected. Neither your face, nor your name, will be seen or known of outside the walls of this room. You may testify with no fear whatsoever, and you can tell us everything you know about the facts you have been a witness to. First of all, I would like you to tell us where you lived in 1993. I would also like you to tell us who the members of your family were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Maybe, Your Honour, we could go into closed session at once so that these elements of information could be given to the Chamber. Mr. Usher, could you please give to Witness FF these documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We are now in closed session. (Closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, I would now like you to tell us more about the period of time that stretches from October 1992, particularly, the conflict which took place in October 1992, and April 1993. First of all, could you tell us for how long you had been living in Ahmici when the events took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: I lived there eight years, from 1985 until 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any relationships with your Croat neighbours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: We would visit. We would come to see one another. We never had any problems. They came to visit us and we went to visit them. We had good relations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us who your closest Croat neighbours were?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the weeks or the months prior to April 1993, did you notice a change in the general atmosphere prevailing in the village? Was there a change in the nature of the relationship between the Muslim community and the Croat community?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: No. There weren't any problems. During those last two or three months, they had started with their preparations, exercises. They walked along the road quite naturally wearing arms, but we never had any complications because of that, until the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Santici area where you lived, was it possible for you to see soldiers very often? Did you see soldiers very often?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: I would often see them when they would walk by. My house was near the main road where all the traffic was, and that is where they usually went out to Donja Rovna and Radakovo (phoen) for their exercises. They were doing their job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Croat neighbours you told us about a moment ago, you also gave their names, did they also take part in these training exercises? Were there also soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: No, not them, but those others went. I never saw them in uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see your Croat neighbours dressed in a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: I saw Drago in uniform. While they stood guard, I would see him. The others, Papic, also Vlado, Nenad, they were also in uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just mentioned Nenad. Could you give us his full name, first and last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: His first name is Nenad, but I can't remember his last name. I can't remember his last name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Drago. Could you give us his full name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Drago Josipovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the days prior to April 16th, 1993, did any particular events take place, events which surprised you or shocked you, maybe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Nothing surprised me. There weren't any problems. It's not that we had some misunderstandings or that we quarrelled. There weren't any problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about your husband, was he quite confidant about the situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: My husband didn't feel very well. He had a suspicion. He said, "Something strange is going on." He said that he felt something in the air. He wasn't well, although I comforted him and said that all would be well and that there wouldn't be any problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he try to explain what feeling he had? Did he tell you about strange things he may have noticed in or around the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: As far as that is concerned, he didn't say anything definite to me, but he only felt the tension. He said, "It's hard to breathe here. I don't feel too good at all."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the eve of April 16th, 1993, i.e., during the day of the 15th or during the night of the 15th of April, did you, yourself, notice something strange in the atmosphere in the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: My husband and I were at (redacted) (redacted), and we were coming back along the field. I saw a few soldiers in front of (redacted) house. They were watching us from up there. We came to our house. That evening, all was quiet. There were no lights on in their houses. Cars passed by often along our road going to Rovna. All was quiet before it started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fact that there were no lights in the Croat houses, was that something unusual?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes, yes, because before, the lights would be on every evening. Naturally, we would see it because they lived nearby. But that evening, you couldn't see lights anywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No lights in the Croat houses. But what about the Muslim houses, were there any lights in these houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes. Naturally, we were in our own houses. We turned the lights on, as we always did. We weren't expecting anything. Naturally, we were at home with our children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now speak about what happened on April 16th, 1993. What are your recollections of what took place during April 16th, 1993, your first recollections of what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: I was awakened by two strong detonations. I got up. My husband got up. I went to the room where my children slept. My older son got up. I took the younger one in my arms. I went back to the room where my husband and I had slept, together with him, and then I went back to my children's bedroom again. I looked through the window. (redacted)house on fire and her mother's house on fire. We didn't know what was going on. We heard shots. I took a sweater to put on. At that moment, a bullet came from my brother-in-law's house through the window, and I felt strange in the head. I ran out of this room to the room where my children were. I told my husband that a bullet had come into the room. He came back, and he said, "Will it set the house on fire? The children are here." He looked for the bullet but he couldn't find it. He came back to me again. We took the children. We carried them to the bathroom. We thought that they would be safe there, that nothing could happen to them there. My father-in-law and mother-in-law were at the entrance. There was a small room there. My husband, my children, and I were in the bathroom. We were quiet. There was a male voice shouting from the outside saying, "If there are any men in here, they should come out." My father-in-law and my mother-in-law went out before we did, and I told my husband that we should go out, that there was nothing to wait for. My husband went out into the hallway. He took his jacket and shoes. I took my younger son in my arms. My husband went out before I did. I remained standing at the door because I didn't dare go out. They shot. They didn't shoot at us. The soldier who stood across from the place where he would lock me up, he held a rifle in his left hand, and he shot into the air. My husband went down the steps. The soldier told me to walk up to him, and I said that I didn't dare to and that I was afraid that someone would kill my children. He answered that no one would do me any harm, that I could come up to him without any fear. I ran across the yard to him. My mother-in-law followed me, and I turned around. I saw my brother-in-law standing in front of his house, and he was shouting to his family members that they should get out of the house too. That soldier opened the door for me. I walked in there, as did my children and my mother-in-law, and he closed the door again. A group had gathered by then. Some of them said that they would go into the house to search for weapons. A soldier had broken glass all over the automobile, and others walked into the room that they had already torched, and it had already started burning. Then my sister-in-law came and her daughter, and they locked them up together with us, and then they set out down there. A few minutes later, it was quiet but I heard five shots, five individual shots, from the shed. Then all went quiet again, and nothing was heard after that. No one was there. They went on further. We were locked up in there until the afternoon. Then, again, we heard someone speaking in the yard. Two soldiers came. They opened the door for us, and they asked, "Why are you there?" We said that we were locked up by their soldiers, and they asked where our husbands were. They asked what happened to them, and I told the soldier what my husband wore. He just looked down to the ground and he didn't answer anything. He told my mother-in-law that a lot of men were taken prisoner and taken to Busovaca. He said, "Perhaps your menfolk are there." This soldier said, "This is Alija Izetbegovic's fault for the war breaking out." We didn't say anything to that. We asked him to bring us some water. He brought us some water. He brought us two blankets from upstairs. He said that we should stay there because he said, "We don't know what to do with you. If another army comes along, they will kill you too." So they locked us up again and we waited. Some time had passed, and they, again, opened the door and they told us to go out into the yard. Josip came; Vinko came; two more soldiers came. I don't remember their names because I did not know everyone. Because we asked where our husbands were, they said that everything would be all right. They said, "More of your women," our women, "went to the cellar of Slavko Vrebac," and they said, "You can go there too." We came to the cellar of Slavko Vrebac. Our other women were there, indeed. Their women were there too. We walked into the cellar, and we saw our women crying. We asked them why they were crying and what was going on, and they said that their husbands and sons were killed and that they saw them as they were going out of the houses. They asked us where our menfolk were, and we didn't know what to answer to that. We spent the night there. They told us, in the morning, that we should leave because it wasn't safe for us there and that they could no longer offer us any protection. We set out over the fields towards Muslim houses, and they were shooting after us. Nothing happened to anyone, though. We came to a Muslim house. A Croat came there and he said, "Don't worry. I'll take you along the road to the entrance to Sivrino Selo, and your people will take you over from there," he said. The column left from there, and we received Sivrino Selo. Our people received us there. We stayed there two evenings. In the morning, we left, setting off towards Poculica. We stayed there for a week. After that, we went down to Zenica, and I stayed there for three months. Then I went through the forest to my mother's, and I lived there. I got a temporary residence in Zenica, so I went back there. That's where I live with my children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. I will ask you a few questions so that everything is perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe this would be a good time to take a break, and that would also enable the witness to rest a little bit. Maybe we could take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Whatever you decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Madam, do you feel the need to take a rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I feel quite all right for the moment. I don't feel bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Then we shall go on. Mr. Usher, could you please put on the ELMO the aerial photograph so that the witness can have a look?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness FF, I will ask you to show us the houses which you saw on fire that morning of the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: This is (redacted) and this is her mother's house, and this is (redacted). I saw the house on fire (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned (redacted)house and (redacted). 14 (redacted). You're thinking of (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes, (redacted), yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you talk about (redacted) house, are you thinking of (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: (redacted) yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see your (redacted) house, 20 (redacted), going into flames?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see soldiers being gathered around the house (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: They were around his barn, his shed, where they fired. They did not shoot at us, but I did not see the soldiers, although there were a lot of them when they shut us up and when they came into our yard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear the soldiers who were around (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: I did not hear them. Because of the noise made by the shooting, I did not hear them. I just heard, when I came up to the entrance and when the soldier was to shut me in there, (redacted) said that his family was going out of the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard a voice. It was a soldier's voice, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: No. I heard (redacted) shouting to his family to come out, and before that, the soldiers called out to me to come out. The soldier who was to have locked me up, I heard his voice when we were in the house. I don't remember whether the others called out to us when they were around (redacted), because there was heavy shooting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were locked up in the barn, you were there, together with your mother-in-law and your two children, can you assess the time which elapsed before your sister-in-law arrived? I think I can mention her first name. I have (redacted) and her daughter in mind.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: (redacted)and (redacted) the daughter. Several minutes elapsed. She came right after us. Not much time had gone by, just a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the condition of these two? In what state were they in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Well, it was quite normal that they were afraid, just as we were. It was frightening. We had no words to express our thoughts. We said nothing to each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, I'd like to show you this diagram.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I mention to the Court that this is not a diagram according to scale. It is just a rough sketch of the buildings.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit 282.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you identify the location of your house in this diagram?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: This is my house (indicating). This was the summer kitchen, the wood storage shed, the garage, and a facility that we had for slaughtering cattle. This was the barn (indicating), and there was a small hut here where I was locked up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you show the location where you were on this diagram when you saw your husband and your brother-in-law being taken away by the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: My father-in-law? The entrance to the upper floor was here (indicating). This was the entrance to the house (indicating). My husband had gone out before me, and my father-in-law went with him. They went across the yard, this way, towards the barn. Then I lost sight of them. I remained standing at the entrance, at the door, until I went up to the soldier who locked me up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to put a cross on that location where you were standing, where you were when your husband and your father-in-law were taken away by the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: (Marks). I was standing at the entrance to my house. This was where the door was (indicating). There were two steps. My husband and father-in-law had gone out across the yard. This was the yard (indicating), and they were taken this way, down here. I stayed here. My husband put on some shoes. At that moment, the soldier called out to me, and I ran across the yard to the place where they shut me in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Madam, could you put a letter "A" on the first cross you put on this diagram. There, where you were standing, put the letter "A," please, if you can?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the record, I shall say that the other three crosses you put on this diagram represent the route taken by your husband and your father-in-law when they were taken away by the soldiers. I'd like to ask you to put a cross and the letter "B" on the location where you went into the barn, to show where the barn door is, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can't see anything on the screen so that I'm not able to follow the testimony of the witness. I'd like this to be made possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. It's difficult to do everything at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. Please put a cross there where you went into the barn, if you can.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then put the letter "B" on that place.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: The place where I put the cross?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed. Then we'll put the diagram back on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could we go back over everything that we said before, because now we have the diagram in front of us and we can follow better. So "A," what is "A"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, everyone can now see the diagram, as well as the crosses you put on it. It might be useful to explain, once more, what these crosses represent. You mentioned a first cross with the letter "A" next to it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: That is the exit, the way out of the house, and that is where we left from. My family, myself, my husband, my father-in-law, and mother-in-law, that's where we went out of the house we lived in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then put another three little crosses towards the left-hand side. What do they represent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: They represent the yard across which my brother-in-law, father-in-law, and husband were taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the way they went when they were taken away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lastly, you put another small cross with the letter "B" next to it. What does that location show?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: The circle indicates the spot to where I came, up to the barn door, where there was a little space inside. I was shut in with my children and my mother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went from your house to the barn where you were locked up, together with your children and your mother-in-law. Did you go straight ahead of you? Was it in a straightforward way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Earlier on, you spoke about gunfire and then five distinct shots. When did you hear them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: When we were shut up. When my in-law came and her daughter, when my husband's brother's wife came with her daughter, several minutes later, I heard five shots, five individual shots, below the barn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see your house on fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FF
utterances.text: After some time had gone by, the room where the bullet entered under (redacted) was ablaze. The room was on fire, and then the summer kitchen, everything began to burn there too immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We have to have a break. The interpreters have been working for over two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Only a few questions, but very few of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We'll have a 30-minute break.
